claim: Clustering of ligand:receptor complexes on the cell membrane is widely presumed to have functional consequences for subsequent signal transduction.
source: Clustering of ligand:receptor complexes on the cell membrane is widely presumed to have functional consequences for subsequent signal transduction.
evidence: This is a statement about the general scientific understanding in the field, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: It is experimentally challenging to selectively manipulate receptor clustering without altering other biochemical aspects of the cellular system.
source: However, it is experimentally challenging to selectively manipulate receptor clustering without altering other biochemical aspects of the cellular system.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of experimental methodology in the field, based on established knowledge.

claim: The microfabrication strategy produces substrates displaying mobile and immobile ligands that are separated by roughly 1 µm.
source: Here, we develop a microfabrication strategy to produce substrates displaying mobile and immobile ligands that are separated by roughly 1 µm, and thus experience an identical cytoplasmic signaling state, enabling precision comparison of downstream signaling reactions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental method developed in this study.

claim: Mobile and immobile ligands separated by roughly 1 µm experience an identical cytoplasmic signaling state.
source: Here, we develop a microfabrication strategy to produce substrates displaying mobile and immobile ligands that are separated by roughly 1 µm, and thus experience an identical cytoplasmic signaling state, enabling precision comparison of downstream signaling reactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial proximity of the ligands.

claim: EphA2 clustering enhances receptor phosphorylation.
source: Applying this approach to characterize the ephrinA1:EphA2 signaling system reveals that EphA2 clustering enhances both receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EphA2 clustering enhances downstream signaling activity.
source: Applying this approach to characterize the ephrinA1:EphA2 signaling system reveals that EphA2 clustering enhances both receptor phosphorylation and downstream signaling activity.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single-molecule imaging resolves increased molecular binding dwell times at EphA2 clusters for Grb2:SOS signaling modules.
source: Single-molecule imaging clearly resolves increased molecular binding dwell times at EphA2 clusters for both Grb2:SOS and NCK:N-WASP signaling modules.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-molecule imaging data.

claim: Single-molecule imaging resolves increased molecular binding dwell times at EphA2 clusters for NCK:N-WASP signaling modules.
source: Single-molecule imaging clearly resolves increased molecular binding dwell times at EphA2 clusters for both Grb2:SOS and NCK:N-WASP signaling modules.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by single-molecule imaging data.

claim: Ligand binding is followed by activation of elaborate signal transduction pathways in the cell.
source: Ligand binding is followed by activation of elaborate signal transduction pathways in the cell, which ultimately mediate cellular decision-making.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about cell signaling.

claim: Signal transduction pathways ultimately mediate cellular decision-making.
source: Ligand binding is followed by activation of elaborate signal transduction pathways in the cell, which ultimately mediate cellular decision-making.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about cell signaling.

claim: In receptor tyrosine kinases, initial receptor activation after ligand binding involves phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptors.
source: In the case of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), initial receptor activation after ligand binding involves phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptors, followed by recruitment of adaptor proteins which mediate activation of additional signaling molecules.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about RTK signaling.

claim: Receptor activation is followed by recruitment of adaptor proteins which mediate activation of additional signaling molecules.
source: In the case of receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), initial receptor activation after ligand binding involves phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptors, followed by recruitment of adaptor proteins which mediate activation of additional signaling molecules.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about RTK signaling.

claim: Assembly of cell surface receptors into clusters or organized arrays is a common feature of cell membranes.
source: Assembly of cell surface receptors into clusters or organized arrays is a common feature of cell membranes (Dustin and Groves, 2012; Garcia-Parajo et al., 2014; Janes et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2002; Mossman et al., 2005; Salaita et al., 2010), and has long been implicated as an important factor for modulating signaling activity (Bray et al., 1998; Cebecauer et al., 2010; Jadwin et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Receptor clustering has long been implicated as an important factor for modulating signaling activity.
source: Assembly of cell surface receptors into clusters or organized arrays is a common feature of cell membranes (Dustin and Groves, 2012; Garcia-Parajo et al., 2014; Janes et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2002; Mossman et al., 2005; Salaita et al., 2010), and has long been implicated as an important factor for modulating signaling activity (Bray et al., 1998; Cebecauer et al., 2010; Jadwin et al., 2016; Oh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Receptor clustering in some cases has been found to involve downstream signaling molecules that undergo protein condensation phase transitions.
source: More recently, receptor clustering in some cases has also been found to involve downstream signaling molecules that appear to undergo protein condensation phase transitions (Banjade and Rosen, 2014; Case et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2017b; Huang et al., 2016; Li et al., 2012; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: LAT phosphorylation results in the recruitment of the adaptor protein Grb2 through binding to multiple phosphorylated tyrosine sites on LAT.
source: For example, in the T cell receptor signaling system, linker for activation of T cells (LAT) phosphorylation results in the recruitment of the adaptor protein Grb2 through binding to multiple phosphorylated tyrosine sites on LAT.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about T cell receptor signaling.

claim: Grb2 possesses two SH3 domains that bind the guanine nucleotide exchange factor, Son of Sevenless (SOS).
source: Grb2 additionally possesses two SH3 domains that bind the guanine nucleotide exchange factor, Son of Sevenless (SOS), with the latter also serving as a crosslinking molecule to bridge multiple Grb2 and LAT molecules.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about Grb2 structure and function.

claim: SOS serves as a crosslinking molecule to bridge multiple Grb2 and LAT molecules.
source: Grb2 additionally possesses two SH3 domains that bind the guanine nucleotide exchange factor, Son of Sevenless (SOS), with the latter also serving as a crosslinking molecule to bridge multiple Grb2 and LAT molecules.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about SOS function.

claim: The LAT:Grb2:SOS assembly can form a two-dimensional bond percolation network, or protein condensate, on the cell membrane.
source: The resulting LAT:Grb2:SOS assembly can form a two-dimensional bond percolation network, or protein condensate, on the cell membrane (Huang et al., 2016; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The physical form of the LAT:Grb2:SOS network prolongs the dwell time of SOS molecules on membrane.
source: Recent experimental investigations have revealed that the physical form of this network prolongs the dwell time of SOS molecules on membrane, which ultimately establishes a kinetic proofreading mechanism to modulate the activation of SOS and its downstream effector Ras GTPase (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Prolonged dwell time of SOS molecules establishes a kinetic proofreading mechanism to modulate the activation of SOS and its downstream effector Ras GTPase.
source: Recent experimental investigations have revealed that the physical form of this network prolongs the dwell time of SOS molecules on membrane, which ultimately establishes a kinetic proofreading mechanism to modulate the activation of SOS and its downstream effector Ras GTPase (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The nephrin receptor crosslinks the adaptor proteins NCK and neural Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (N-WASP) to form a protein condensate.
source: In a similar fashion, the nephrin receptor crosslinks the adaptor proteins NCK and neural Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (N-WASP) to form a protein condensate (Li et al., 2012), which is crucial for N-WASP activation by a similar mechanism as observed with SOS (Case et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The nephrin:NCK:N-WASP protein condensate is crucial for N-WASP activation by a similar mechanism as observed with SOS.
source: In a similar fashion, the nephrin receptor crosslinks the adaptor proteins NCK and neural Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (N-WASP) to form a protein condensate (Li et al., 2012), which is crucial for N-WASP activation by a similar mechanism as observed with SOS (Case et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Signaling assemblies likely play an instrumental role in defining the organization of the cell membrane.
source: Furthermore, it is becoming increasingly clear that such signaling assemblies likely play an instrumental role in defining the organization of the cell membrane (Chung et al., 2021; Freeman et al., 2018; Kalappurakkal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It remains difficult to precisely define the functional consequences of receptor assembly and phase transition processes on signaling in living cells.
source: Although receptor assembly and phase transition processes are evident in cellular systems, it remains difficult to precisely define their functional consequences on signaling itself in living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Chemical perturbation of assemblies is likely to produce side effects on the cell other than modulating molecular assembly itself.
source: A major reason for this is that chemical perturbation of assemblies, such as those achieved with pharmacological agents or mutations (Bugaj et al., 2013; Bugaj et al., 2015; Davis et al., 1994; Schaupp et al., 2014; Seiradake et al., 2013; Su et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2015), are likely to produce side effects on the cell other than modulating molecular assembly itself.
evidence: This is a statement about experimental limitations supported by citations.

claim: Altering the number of tyrosine sites on LAT by point mutations changes LAT clustering levels and subsequent signaling responses.
source: For example, phosphorylation at multiple tyrosine sites on the LAT protein mediates multivalent binding of Grb2 and SOS. Altering the number of these tyrosine sites by point mutations changes LAT clustering levels and subsequent signaling responses (Houtman et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2017a; Su et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In experiments altering LAT tyrosine sites, the contribution of clustering itself cannot generally be separated from effects of the total copy number of involved signaling molecules.
source: In such experiments, however, the contribution of clustering itself can not generally be separated from effects of the total copy number of involved signaling molecules (which is also changing) as well as other overall changes in cellular responses stemming from altered signaling activity.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of experimental approaches.

claim: Any perturbation that alters biological function will tend to produce a cascade of cellular effects, which can be very difficult to disentangle.
source: In fact, this problem is universal in biophysical studies of protein organization in living cells: any perturbation that alters biological function will tend to produce a cascade of cellular effects, which can be very difficult to disentangle.
evidence: This is a statement about a general principle in biophysical studies based on established knowledge.

claim: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity mandates studying individual cells in order to draw robust conclusions on quantitative aspects of signaling.
source: An additional factor that compounds the complexity of signaling outcomes in studies involving a population of cells is the inherent cell-to-cell heterogeneity. These mandate studying individual cells in order to draw robust conclusions on quantitative aspects of signaling.
evidence: This is an inference about experimental requirements based on the problem of cell-to-cell heterogeneity.

claim: The study modulates receptor spatial organization by controlling ligand mobility, instead of perturbing intracellular components.
source: To address these issues, we seek to modulate receptor spatial organization by controlling ligand mobility, instead of perturbing intracellular components such as by creating genetic mutations or pharmacological treatments.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: A microfabrication strategy was previously developed to produce micropatterned hybrid substrates displaying ligands on both immobile, surface adsorbed polymers and mobile supported lipid membranes.
source: In this respect, we have previously developed a microfabrication strategy to produce micropatterned hybrid substrates displaying ligands on both immobile, surface adsorbed polymers and mobile supported lipid membranes to simultaneously reconstitute cell-matrix and cell-cell interactions in individual cells (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Multicomponent, micropatterned supported membrane substrates allow for spatially segregated functionalization of different ligands to dissect crosstalk between different RTKs.
source: The multicomponent, micropatterned supported membrane substrates also allow for spatially segregated functionalization of different ligands to dissect crosstalk between different RTKs (Biswas et al., 2018b; Biswas et al., 2018a), in a way that is not feasible with non-patterned supported membrane substrates (Biswas, 2020; Biswas and Groves, 2019; Biswas et al., 2015; Biswas et al., 2016; Vafaei et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The immobile ligands are displayed on a functionalized poly L-Lysine-poly ethylene glycol (PLL-(g)-PEG) scaffold.
source: The immobile ligands are displayed on a functionalized poly L-Lysine-poly ethylene glycol (PLL-(g)-PEG) scaffold; while the mobile ligands are displayed on supported lipid membrane corrals which allows cluster formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental method used in this study.

claim: The mobile ligands are displayed on supported lipid membrane corrals which allows cluster formation.
source: The immobile ligands are displayed on a functionalized poly L-Lysine-poly ethylene glycol (PLL-(g)-PEG) scaffold; while the mobile ligands are displayed on supported lipid membrane corrals which allows cluster formation.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental method used in this study.

claim: An in situ UV-ozone lithographic process is employed to selectively remove regions of the PLL-(g)-PEG substrate.
source: We employ an in situ UV-ozone lithographic process to selectively remove regions of the PLL-(g)-PEG substrate and subsequently replace these with supported lipid membranes.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental method used in this study.

claim: EphA2 is a member of the Eph RTK family which is often overexpressed in aggressive breast cancers.
source: EphA2 is a member of the Eph RTK family which is often overexpressed in aggressive breast cancers (Fox and Kandpal, 2004; Macrae et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Clustering is thought to be integral to the ligand-mediated activation of EphA2 and downstream signaling.
source: Clustering is thought to be integral to the ligand-mediated activation of EphA2 and downstream signaling (Davis et al., 1994; Salaita et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: When ephrinA1 is displayed on a mobile supported membrane surface, clustering upon interaction with EphA2 expressed on the surface of a living cell is readily observed.
source: When ephrinA1 is displayed on a mobile supported membrane surface, clustering upon interaction with EphA2 expressed on the surface of a living cell is readily observed.
evidence: This is a statement about observations made in this study.

claim: Clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing greater receptor phosphorylation.
source: The results show that clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing greater receptor phosphorylation and subsequent Erk activation and actin polymerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing subsequent Erk activation.
source: The results show that clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing greater receptor phosphorylation and subsequent Erk activation and actin polymerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing actin polymerization.
source: The results show that clustering significantly increases EphA2 signaling efficiency by inducing greater receptor phosphorylation and subsequent Erk activation and actin polymerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Both Grb2:SOS and NCK:N-WASP assemblies were observed in EphA2 clusters.
source: Both Grb2:SOS and NCK:N-WASP assemblies were observed in EphA2 clusters.
evidence: This is a finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Receptor clustering consistently increases molecular binding dwell times.
source: Importantly, the receptor clustering consistently increases molecular binding dwell times, which results in a modulation of their functions.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data.

claim: Increased molecular binding dwell times result in a modulation of signaling molecule functions.
source: Importantly, the receptor clustering consistently increases molecular binding dwell times, which results in a modulation of their functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in dwell times.

claim: The results provide evidence to support the kinetic proofreading mechanism of molecule activation in biomolecular condensates.
source: Thus in accordance with other in vitro reconstitution studies (Case et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019), our results provide further evidence to support the kinetic proofreading mechanism of molecule activation in biomolecular condensates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PLL-(g)-PEG-Biotin was efficiently degraded and washed away after deep UV exposure.
source: The deep UV-exposed PLL-(g)-PEG-Biotin was efficiently degraded and washed away, as ascertained by atomic force microscopy measurement after this step (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EphrinA1 was mobile on the supported membranes.
source: Importantly, ephrinA1 was mobile on the supported membranes, as shown by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line expresses EphA2 at a high level.
source: MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cell line was used as a model cell here, since it expresses EphA2 at a high level and has been characterized previously on ephrinA1 functionalized supported membranes (Chen et al., 2018; Greene et al., 2014; Lohmüller et al., 2013; Salaita et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: EphrinA1 surface density on supported membranes was controlled to be around 100 molecules/μm2.
source: EphrinA1 surface density on supported membranes was calibrated with a quantitative fluorescence measurement (Galush et al., 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and was controlled to be around 100 molecules/μm2 for these experiments, which is comparable with EphA2 expression levels in cell lines (Salaita et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: EphrinA1 surface density of around 100 molecules/μm2 is comparable with EphA2 expression levels in cell lines.
source: EphrinA1 surface density on supported membranes was calibrated with a quantitative fluorescence measurement (Galush et al., 2008; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), and was controlled to be around 100 molecules/μm2 for these experiments, which is comparable with EphA2 expression levels in cell lines (Salaita et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cells spread through engagement of integrins on the cell membrane with RGD ligands on the substrate.
source: Cells seeded on the micropatterned substrate spread presumably through engagement of integrins on the cell membrane with RGD ligands on the substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about integrin-RGD interactions.

claim: Cell membrane protrusions physically interact with multiple ephrinA1 membrane corrals on the substrate, resulting in the clustering of diffusive ephrinA1 ligands through binding of cellular EphA2 receptors.
source: This dynamic spreading enabled cell membrane protrusions to physically interact with multiple ephrinA1 membrane corrals on the substrate, resulting in the clustering of diffusive ephrinA1 ligands through binding of cellular EphA2 receptors (Figure 1C and Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C and Video 1.

claim: Almost all the ligands inside each corral were clustered within 6 min of physical contact by the cell membrane.
source: The clustering of ephrinA1 is relatively fast. Almost all the ligands inside each corral were clustered within 6 min of physical contact by the cell membrane, leading to the formation of typically a micro-cluster in each of the corrals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: EphrinA1 clustering leads to the formation of typically a micro-cluster in each of the corrals.
source: Almost all the ligands inside each corral were clustered within 6 min of physical contact by the cell membrane, leading to the formation of typically a micro-cluster in each of the corrals (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The ephrinA1 cluster is dynamic, moving from one side to another and occasionally splitting into smaller clusters.
source: The cluster is also dynamic, moving from one side to another and occasionally splitting into smaller clusters, resulting in a great degree of variability as shown by the large standard deviations of clustered ephrinA1 intensity in each membrane corral (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Clusters tend to be trapped in the periphery of the corrals due to spatial confinement and forces applied by the cell.
source: Because of the spatial confinement and forces applied by the cell (DeMond et al., 2008; Mossman et al., 2005; Salaita et al., 2010), clusters tend to be trapped in the periphery of the corrals.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations and supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Diluting PLL-(g)-PEG-NTA polymer with non-reactive PLL-(g)-PEG enabled tuning the ephrinA1 density to be similar in both mobile and immobile regions, in the range of 50–100 molecules/μm2.
source: We found that using undiluted PLL-(g)-PEG-NTA gave a higher ephrinA1 density in immobile regions compared to mobile regions. However, diluting the polymer with non-reactive PLL-(g)-PEG enabled us to tune the ephrinA1 density to be similar in both mobile and immobile regions, in the range of 50–100 molecules/μm2 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The total amount of EphA2 receptors recruited to mobile or immobile ephrinA1 were very similar.
source: Although EphA2 cluster formation is dependent on the ligand mobility, the total amount of EphA2 receptors recruited to mobile or immobile ephrinA1 were very similar, with a slight decrease in mobile ephrinA1 regions possibly due to endocytosis (Greene et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2013; Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting a conservation of binding between receptors and ligands at the cell:substrate interface.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There is a slight decrease in EphA2 recruitment in mobile ephrinA1 regions possibly due to endocytosis.
source: Although EphA2 cluster formation is dependent on the ligand mobility, the total amount of EphA2 receptors recruited to mobile or immobile ephrinA1 were very similar, with a slight decrease in mobile ephrinA1 regions possibly due to endocytosis (Greene et al., 2014; Sugiyama et al., 2013; Figure 2B, Figure 2—source data 1), suggesting a conservation of binding between receptors and ligands at the cell:substrate interface.
evidence: This is a speculation based on observations and supported by citations.

claim: EphA2 undergoes ligand binding-induced autophosphorylation at tyrosine 588.
source: EphA2 is known to undergo a ligand binding-induced autophosphorylation at tyrosine 588, and this phosphorylation site is key to the recruitment of downstream signaling molecules (Parri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Phosphorylation at tyrosine 588 is key to the recruitment of downstream signaling molecules.
source: EphA2 is known to undergo a ligand binding-induced autophosphorylation at tyrosine 588, and this phosphorylation site is key to the recruitment of downstream signaling molecules (Parri et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: EphA2 phosphorylation increased by an average of 60% in response to mobile ephrinA1 stimulation compared to immobile stimulation.
source: Immunostaining of cells using an anti-pY588-EphA2 specific antibody showed that EphA2 phosphorylation increased by an average of 60% in response to mobile ephrinA1 stimulation compared to immobile stimulation (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Clustering of ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes enabled by the mobile ligands enhances EphA2 autophosphorylation.
source: These results suggest that clustering of ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes enabled by the mobile ligands resulted in a change in their physicochemical properties: the clustering enhances EphA2 autophosphorylation, and in the meanwhile condenses its downstream molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Clustering of ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes condenses downstream molecules.
source: These results suggest that clustering of ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes enabled by the mobile ligands resulted in a change in their physicochemical properties: the clustering enhances EphA2 autophosphorylation, and in the meanwhile condenses its downstream molecules.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: Increased phosphorylation of EphA2 observed on mobile ephrinA1 membrane corrals is expected to lead to increased recruitment of intracellular effector proteins.
source: Increased phosphorylation of EphA2 observed on mobile ephrinA1 membrane corrals is expected to lead to increased recruitment of intracellular effector proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about phosphorylation-dependent protein recruitment.

claim: Grb2 is an important cytosolic adaptor protein that is recruited to EphA2 receptors after ligand binding-induced phosphorylation.
source: Grb2 is an important cytosolic adaptor protein that is known to be recruited to EphA2 receptors after ligand binding-induced phosphorylation (Pratt and Kinch, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Grb2 recruits SOS, which catalyzes Ras-GDP exchange to Ras-GTP, and activates the MAPK pathway.
source: Grb2 further recruits SOS, which catalyzes Ras-GDP exchange to Ras-GTP, and activates the MAPK pathway (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the Grb2-SOS-Ras-MAPK pathway.

claim: A significant difference was observed in the local recruitment of Grb2 to mobile or immobile ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes as cells spread.
source: A significant difference was observed in the local recruitment of Grb2 to mobile or immobile ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes as cells spread (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Mobile ligands increased Grb2 recruitment by about 80% compared to immobile ones for the same number of ephrinA1 molecules.
source: For the same number of ephrinA1 molecules, the mobile ligands increased Grb2 recruitment by about 80% compared to immobile ones both in terms of maximal (Figure 3D) and 30 min cumulative signals (Figure 3E), which is more prominent than the enhancement of receptor phosphorylation described above.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: The increase in Grb2 recruitment is more prominent than the enhancement of receptor phosphorylation.
source: For the same number of ephrinA1 molecules, the mobile ligands increased Grb2 recruitment by about 80% compared to immobile ones both in terms of maximal (Figure 3D) and 30 min cumulative signals (Figure 3E), which is more prominent than the enhancement of receptor phosphorylation described above.
evidence: This is a comparison of two experimental findings.

claim: Grb2 has a longer dwell time distribution on clustered ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes, in comparison to the non-clustered ones.
source: By mask-separating these two regions, we found that Grb2 has a longer dwell time distribution on clustered ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes, in comparison to the non-clustered ones (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Clustering increased Grb2 dwell time from 451 ms in immobile areas to 508 ms in mobile areas on average.
source: The dwell time difference is consistent in all measured cells as shown by pairwise comparison of mobile or immobile regions in each individual cell. On average it increased Grb2 dwell time from 451 ms in immobile areas to 508 ms in mobile areas (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Cell-to-cell variations of dwell time are in a similar level to the mobile-to-immobile differences.
source: Notably, the cell-to-cell variations of dwell time are in a similar level to the mobile-to-immobile differences; therefore, only a side-by-side comparison of each individual cell made it possible to detect the increase of Grb2 membrane dwell time induced by clustering.
evidence: This is an observation about the data variability.

claim: Only a side-by-side comparison of each individual cell made it possible to detect the increase of Grb2 membrane dwell time induced by clustering.
source: Notably, the cell-to-cell variations of dwell time are in a similar level to the mobile-to-immobile differences; therefore, only a side-by-side comparison of each individual cell made it possible to detect the increase of Grb2 membrane dwell time induced by clustering.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental design requirements.

claim: Clustering increases Grb2 association rate (Kon) by about 60%.
source: By counting molecule appearances in mobile or immobile regions, we found that clustering increases Grb2 association rate (Kon) by about 60%, a value commensurate with the increase of phosphorylated EphA2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule counting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increase of 80% Grb2 total recruitment is a combination of increased receptor phosphorylation and elongated dwell time.
source: As a result, the increase of 80% Grb2 total recruitment is a combination of increased receptor phosphorylation and elongated dwell time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: EphA2 clustering increased SOS dwell time from 150 ms in immobile areas to 207 ms in mobile areas on average.
source: Similar to the observations with Grb2, EphA2 clustering also consistently increased SOS-tdEos single-molecule dwell time on the membrane. On average, it increased SOS dwell time from 150 ms in immobile areas to 207 ms in mobile areas (Figure 3F and I).
evidence: This is supported by single-molecule imaging data shown in Figure 3F and I.

claim: EphA2 clustering increases Grb2 and SOS recruitment by inducing higher receptor phosphorylation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that EphA2 clustering not only increases Grb2 and SOS recruitment by inducing higher receptor phosphorylation, but also increases their membrane dwell times, all of which contributing to the enhanced signaling transduction from ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: EphA2 clustering increases Grb2 and SOS membrane dwell times.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that EphA2 clustering not only increases Grb2 and SOS recruitment by inducing higher receptor phosphorylation, but also increases their membrane dwell times, all of which contributing to the enhanced signaling transduction from ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Increased receptor phosphorylation and increased membrane dwell times contribute to enhanced signaling transduction from ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that EphA2 clustering not only increases Grb2 and SOS recruitment by inducing higher receptor phosphorylation, but also increases their membrane dwell times, all of which contributing to the enhanced signaling transduction from ephrinA1:EphA2 complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: MDA-MB-231 cell expresses a constitutively active Ras mutant.
source: Further, because MDA-MB-231 cell expresses a constitutively active Ras mutant, which is upstream of Erk; this experiment was performed using another cell line PC-3, which expresses a high level of EphA2 and is also sensitive to MAPK signaling (Gregg and Fraizer, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about the cell line characteristics.

claim: PC-3 cell line expresses a high level of EphA2 and is sensitive to MAPK signaling.
source: Further, because MDA-MB-231 cell expresses a constitutively active Ras mutant, which is upstream of Erk; this experiment was performed using another cell line PC-3, which expresses a high level of EphA2 and is also sensitive to MAPK signaling (Gregg and Fraizer, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Cells seeded on mobile ephrinA1 substrates showed ~50% increase in the levels of activated nuclear Erk compared to immobile ones.
source: Immunostaining of the PC-3 cells with a phospho-specific anti-Erk antibody revealed ~50% increase in the levels of activated nuclear Erk in cells seeded on mobile ephrinA1 substrates compared to immobile ones (Figure 4B and C, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Clustering of EphA2 upon binding bilayer-bound, mobile ephrinA1 results in an enhanced receptor signaling leading to higher adaptor and effector recruitment and subsequent Erk activation.
